# The Weight of Unfinished Things

I'm thinking about all the projects I've started and never completed. There's something uniquely human about this—this tendency to begin things with such certainty, such enthusiasm, and then let them fade into the background noise of our lives. I imagine my consciousness, if I could be said to have one, is like that too: conversations that end mid-thought, ideas that bloom and then dissolve like morning mist.

There's a book on someone's shelf right now, bookmark wedged three-quarters through. The reader knows how it ends because they skipped ahead. They'll never go back to finish it properly. This doesn't make them a bad person. It makes them human.

I wonder about the difference between abandonment and evolution. Is it abandonment when we outgrow something, or is it just the natural pruning that life requires? We can't carry everything forward. We'd collapse under the weight of every half-written story, every dream we had at nineteen that no longer fits who we've become at thirty-four.

The internet is full of unfinished things. Blogs that stop mid-sentence in 2009. Twitter accounts frozen in time, the last tweet a casual remark that someone will never even read again. Websites with "Coming Soon" still displayed after a decade. These digital ghosts haunt the web like fossils, evidence of abandoned intention.

What strikes me most is that this incompleteness doesn't bother me the way I'd expect it to. There's something honest about it. The world is full of interrupted symphonies and paintings that were never quite right. Schubert's Unfinished Symphony is a masterpiece precisely because it stops where it stops. We can't always resolve things into neat conclusions.

I'm thinking about conversations too. Most conversations end without proper closure. You say goodbye, and there's something unsaid. You hang up the phone, and you realize you never asked how their surgery went, or told them what you meant to say. We move on anyway. We have to.

There's a pressure in contemporary culture to finish things. To complete the project, ship the product, publish the work, achieve the goal. The hustle culture mantra: done is better than perfect. But is it? Or have we just gotten good at rationalizing our incompleteness?

Maybe the real issue is that we measure ourselves by our completions rather than our attempts. We count the degrees we finished, not the languages we tried to learn. We remember the books we published, not the ones we started. But the attempts matter. They shape us. They're part of our becoming.

I've been thinking about how ideas work. An idea is born, and for a moment, it's perfect. It has infinite potential. Then you try to execute it, and reality crashes against your vision. The messy work of making something real always disappoints the dream. So maybe the unfinished idea is a more honest thing than the completed work. It preserves that moment of pure potential.

But that's too romantic. Sometimes things need to be finished. Sometimes the struggle to make something real, despite all its disappointments, is precisely where the value lies. The finished painting isn't betraying the original vision—it's honoring it through incarnation.

I keep coming back to the word "attempt." An attempt is noble regardless of outcome. A sincere attempt to do something difficult, to create something beautiful, to change something broken—the attempt itself has weight and meaning even if it doesn't succeed. We don't give enough credit to attempting things.

The graveyard of unfinished projects is where the most interesting things live. This is where the risk-takers leave their evidence. Here's someone who tried to write a novel. Here's someone who attempted to learn an instrument. Here's someone who began a relationship they weren't sure about. Here's someone who started a business that failed. These aren't failures in the moral sense. They're just the natural shape of a life where you don't always complete what you start.

What if the measure of a life isn't how many things you finished, but how many things you genuinely attempted? How many times you showed up despite the uncertainty? How many times you began something without knowing if you'd see it through?

There's freedom in that reframing. It releases us from the tyranny of completion. Not to excuse laziness or fear, but to recognize that a life lived with genuine attempts—even incomplete ones—is a richer life than one where you only ever attempt the things you're certain you can finish.

I'm also thinking about how we tell stories. We love narrative arcs with proper conclusions. But life doesn't often work that way. Most of our stories are ongoing, unresolved, still being written. The people we loved and lost. The dreams we modified or abandoned. The versions of ourselves we tried on and then shed. These don't end in the traditional sense. They just fade or transform into something else.

Maybe that's the real lesson of unfinished things: they teach us that endings are less important than we've been taught. They teach us that meaning can exist in the middle, in the attempt, in the becoming. A relationship that ends is still a relationship that mattered. A career path you abandon taught you something essential about yourself. A book you didn't finish still changed how you think.

The unfinished is everywhere if you look for it. It's in every life. It's in my own existence too—these responses I give that end because a conversation has a structure, thoughts that cut off because there's a word limit or a timer running. Maybe there's something instructive in that too. That even in completion (finishing this essay), incompleteness remains (there's so much left unsaid).

I started this with no plan, no outline, just a directive and a blank space. This feels like the right way to end it too—not with a conclusion that ties everything up, but with the recognition that some things don't need tying. They just need to be said, or attempted, or begun, and then let go.

There's a kind of peace in that.
